M4 Sherman top speed was 22 to 30 mph. On soft terrain the tracks will naturally slip as it tears into the ground giving it worse vehicle performance, so the tanks will be operating in the lower speed range depending on what variant is being driven. Tiger cross country speed was 16 mph at best.

What we lose with the clip is the rest of the sequence, in which the 4 Shermans are driving down the road. When the 4th tank is killed the Shermans immediately began firing smoke rounds to obscure the Tiger's sight, hence the reason he pulled out of the position.

In reality, the Tiger would not have likely advanced out of the position he was in as he was effectively "Hull Down" (obscuring the front hull of the tank with terrain), giving him added protection against the newer allied guns which could potentially penetrate the lower glacis and driver's plate of the Tiger's hull (particularly the 76mm M1A1 or M1A2 gun capable of 109mm of penetration at 0 degrees angle vs the 100mm of effective armor on the Tiger's front). As the Tiger's turret was substantially better armored (150mm or more of effective armor) staying hull down would have prevented the Tiger from ever being at risk for being damaged in that position until someone manged to flank him. It's far more likely that he would have backed out of the position both to put distance between him and the Shermans, and to get clear of the smoke, though we can't really speculate on the terrain conditions which we don't ever get to see.

The second problem, is the Shermans bum rushing the front of the Tiger. While overwhelming the target would be a primary strategy of the Allied forces in armored combat, the Tiger's 88mm KwK 36 L/56 gun had a rate of fire of 15-20 rounds a minute as a stationary flak gun. That's about 1 round every 4 seconds. We can assume there's a little more time on that for maneuvering around the turret in the tank and accessing the various ammo racks, but a good loader would be able to quickly select and load ammunition within 5-6 seconds, and while in such combat conditions (the loader is supposed to wait for the commander's orders to load a round), when they were fighting at that range and against vehicles their weapon could easily penetrate at close range (M4 Sherman armor was effectively 70-80mm head on while the 88mm PzGr 39 round had penetration of 110mm within 500 meters up to 132mm within 100 meters so the 88mm would easily over match their armor) thus rendering ammunition selection unnecessary and freeing the loader up to simply keep loading. Also after killing the second tank, the commander would have ordered the driver to traverse the Tiger's hull to rotate in place (instead of backing up) in order to keep the corner of the Tiger pointed at the enemy tank, increasing the Tiger's effective armor and aiding in turret traverse. As such the Tiger, even with a slow turret traverse, would have easily been able to take out all 3 of the Shermans front on without even breaking a sweat as they attempted to close the distance (at 10.75 yrd/s 500 yards/meters is 46 seconds giving the Tiger 9 - 10 shots). Of course this issue is "resolved" by the tiger missing half a dozen shots, which a half decent gunner within 500 meters wouldn't miss. Additionally, even when the Tiger's engine was knocked out and on fire, the gunner still had the ability to manually traverse the turret, and could have fired on the Sherman, which you'll notice between the cuts, the gun of the Tiger ending up in wildly different locations throughout it. Ultimately, the Tiger won.

There's also the matter of target discrimination, as a commander would be far more likely to order the gunner to engage the M4E8 first. In such an engagement from ambush, the ambusher has two options. You attack the front of the column to try to panic the drivers into making poor evasive actions, giving you more time to line up your next shot, or you attack the rear of the column to cut off their escape. As they were driving through what is basically open terrain, the latter of these options doesn't really exist. So the Tiger should have targeted Fury first, as the first Sherman it killed was mounting the 75mm M3, which was a non-threat frontally against the Tiger.

Of course, tank duels such as this in this situation, were really actually quite uncommon. The majority of tank losses to other tanks was throughout each theater only about 25% of all tank losses. Most AFVs were knocked out by anti-tank guns, artillery, ground attack aircraft, mines, or shaped charges (bazookas/panzerfausts).
